Abstract 
Aim: The study aims to investigate how SAP S/4HANA’s in-memory database architecture 
achieves exceptionally high processing speeds by examining the HANA database layer, where 
most SAP system performance challenges originate. It further seeks to analyze how columnar 
storage, compression techniques, set-based programming, indexing, and data-partitioning 
strategies contribute to overall system efficiency, scalability, and real-time analytics. 
Methods: The research is grounded in SAP HANA architecture documentation, S/4HANA 
developer manuals, and established performance-engineering literature. A practical assessment 
was conducted using representative SQL queries, CDS Views, and SQL Scripts executed directly 
on SAP HANA. Performance-analysis tools included ST05, ST12, SAT, DBACOCKPIT, and 
PlanViz to evaluate memory usage, indexing behavior, execution paths, and runtime performance. 
Results: The study reveals that SAP S/4HANA’s columnar storage model significantly enhances 
selective data retrieval, while dictionary and vector-based compression reduce memory footprint 
and accelerate data access. Storing operational data entirely in main memory enables simultaneous 
execution of transactional and analytical workloads. Set-based processing through CDS Views and 
SQL Script is shown to outperform traditional ABAP loop-based logic, reinforcing the 
effectiveness of shifting computations to the database layer. Additionally, partitioning strategies 
such as round-robin, hash, and range partitioning enable parallel execution and even distribution 
of large datasets across processing threads, improving scalability and sustaining performance 
under heavy workloads.  
Conclusion: The study concludes that SAP S/4HANA’s in-memory design combined with 
columnar processing, advanced compression, database-driven logic, and optimized indexing and 
partitioning forms the foundation of its real-time processing capability.  
Recommendation: To fully leverage S/4HANA’s performance potential, developers and solution 
architects should adopt set-based programming practices, apply appropriate indexing and 
partitioning strategies, and rely on database-side execution wherever possible.  
Keywords: SAP S/4HANA, in-memory computing, database performance optimization, real-time 
analytics, columnar storage, set-based processing, parallel processing, pushdown processing, 
table partitioning

1. INTRODUCTION 
Performance in SAP systems is affected by three interdependent layers: the database layer, the 
application layer, and the infrastructure layer. Understanding and being willing to work on 
optimizing each layer is necessary to achieve sustainable performance in S/4 HANA environments. 
Practically all Fiori apps and SAP transactions require reading or updating stored data; the database 
layer is an essential component of system performance. Every query in traditional databases adds 
latency because it reads and writes data from physical storage.  S/4 HANA works on an in-memory 
database [1]. By storing entire tables, indexes, and intermediate results in RAM and only 
occasionally writing to disk for persistence or backup, in-memory databases remove that 
bottleneck.  
The memory-resident architecture of SAP S/4HANA enables data access in microseconds as 
compared to milliseconds, resulting in a fundamental change in the processing of enterprise 
workloads. The system can retrieve and manipulate massive amounts of data with almost 
instantaneous responsiveness by removing disk and I/O as a bottleneck. Even when thousands of 
users are active at once, this acceleration allows business transactions to be completed in less than 
a second. Additionally, high-throughput processing is supported by in-memory storage, enabling 
real-time analytical queries, aggregations, and computations without affecting transactional 
workloads. Additionally, the architecture facilitates mixed transactional and analytical processing 
(HTAP), which allows businesses to examine operational data in real time without having to wait 
for batch extraction or replication. Also, complex SQL Script logic and CDS Views involving 
joins, filters, and aggregations on large datasets perform better when access times are microsecond-
level. In situations involving real-time dashboards, predictive analytics, and Fiori applications that 
need instant user feedback, this performance advantage becomes more significant. The decreased 
latency guarantees improved system scalability, enabling S/4HANA to sustain steady performance 
as data volumes increase. Overall, S/4HANA’s ability to support real-time, high-performance 
transactional and analytical operations in parallel is primarily made possible by the significant 
reduction in data retrieval time.

The internal workings of SAP S/4 HANA and its in-memory architecture are depicted in the 
diagram. How users and apps connect to the system and manage their sessions is handled by the 
Connection and Session Management section at the top. Only authorized users can view or alter 
data due to the Authorization Manager. The Calculation Engine handles queries sent by users or 
applications using SQL, SQL Script, or MDX and does the necessary computations. The Execution 
Engine executes the plan that the Optimizer and Plan Generator discovered as the fastest way to 
run each query. The central component of SAP S/4 HANA is the In-Memory Processing Engines. 
They process data directly in memory, which is much faster than using a disk. Normal structured 
data, such as tables, is handled by the Column/Row Engine; relationships between data, such as 
networks or hierarchies, are analyzed by the Graph Engine; and full-text searches and language-
based queries are handled by the Text Engine. To ensure consistency, the Metadata Manager 
monitors all data definitions, structures, and relationships. When numerous users are working 
simultaneously, the Transaction Manager ensures that every action is carried out accurately and 
securely. To ensure that no data is lost in the event of a system crash or restart, the Persistence 
Layer uses logging, recovery, and storage to save data permanently [2]. A high-efficiency system 
with significant throughput, rapid data processing, and real-time analytical capabilities that are not 
possible using traditional disk-driven technologies is made possible by these architectural 
components.

Most current research explains how SAP HANA functions, but it doesn’t offer actual performance 
metrics in S/4HANA systems. They describe features like pushdown, indexing, compression, and 
columnar storage, but they don’t examine how these optimizations impact runtime. Indexing and 
partitioning are mentioned in studies, but their effects on various workloads and data volumes are 
not examined. Many papers do not use SAP tools like ST05, ST12, SAT, DBACOCKPIT, or Plan 
Viz to assess performance. Instead, they discuss in-memory concepts at a high level. There is no 
unified framework that explains how query design, indexing, compression, and partitioning work 
together in S/4HANA. Real enterprise workloads, where numerous users and massive data 
volumes perform mixed OLTP and OLAP operations, are rarely studied in the literature. A 
practical, hands-on study is required to demonstrate how SAP S/4HANA’s in-memory 
optimizations enhance performance in actual systems due to these gaps. 
3. METHODOLOGY 
The design focuses on documenting how storage structures, compression, indexing, and 
partitioning influence runtime behavior. The study is based on peer-reviewed research on in-
memory databases and HTAP systems, as well as authoritative SAP HANA architecture 
documentation and S/4HANA developer manuals. These resources offer theoretical support as 
well as practical knowledge. When combined, they guarantee that the analysis is backed by 
established theories and research that has been verified by academics. Using typical SQL queries, 
CDS Views, and SQL Script procedures, practical experiments were carried out on SAP HANA.

4. THE FUNDAMENTALS OF IN-MEMORY DATA ADMINISTRATION 
Instead of using conventional disk drives, an in-memory database is a kind of database 
management system that  
stores data directly in main memory (RAM) [3]. This design allows for real-time data processing, 
analytics, and transactional performance that greatly outperforms traditional systems because 
memory access is significantly faster than disk access. The primary characteristics of an in-
memory database are, 
4.1. Columnar Data Storage 
Unlike traditional systems, which store data row by row, SAPHANA’s in-memory database stores 
data column by column. For instance: 
 
Figure 2: How a Column Store Table is Stored Physically 
For example, the Orders table in the image above has four columns. OrderID, Amount, 
Shipping_country, and CustomerID. All the data in OrderID is stored first.  Then the CustomerID 
data is stored, and so on. The Dictionary and Vector concept is used by HANA to improve CPU 
and memory utilization, speed up data access, and compress data. Dictionary is a lookup table that 
contains all of the distinct values for every column is called a dictionary. HANA generates a 
distinct Dictionary table for every table column rather than storing raw values repeatedly in 
memory. Each column’s raw values are saved by HANA in the corresponding Dictionary table 
[4].  Figure 3 shows how the dictionary table appears.

In what ways do vectors and dictionaries facilitate faster data access? 
Query 1: SELECT SUM(Amount) AS TotalSales FROM Orders. 
 To obtain all of the Value IDs for the Amount field, the CBO (Cost-Based Optimizer) first consults 
the vector table. The actual values of these IDs are then stored in the database cache after being 
looked up in the dictionary table. Lastly, the system swiftly and efficiently sends the result back 
to the application server by using the SUM function on these cached values. 
Query 2: SELECT OrderID, Amount FROM Orders where Shipping_Country = ‘IN’.   
 The Value ID for “IN,” which is 1, is first determined by the CBO using the dictionary table. The 
vector table is then searched to find all records with Shipping Country = 1 (in this case, records 0, 
2, and 4). The Value IDs for the OrderID and Amount fields are then obtained from those records. 
Following the collection of these values, the CBO puts the entire set of records together using the 
vector table and database cache. The result set is then returned to the application server for 
processing or display. 
How is Column Store fetch faster than Row Store? 
Consider a table called ORDERS that has 100,000,000 rows having columns: Amount (8-byte 
decimal), OrderDate (8-byte), Country (dictionary-encoded; code 1 byte), OrderID (4-byte int), 
CustomerID (4-byte int), and five additional miscellaneous columns with an average of 8 bytes 
each. In a row store, the approximate row width is ≈ 4+4+1+8+8 + (5×8) = 69 bytes, which rounds 
up to 72 bytes. 
Ex: SELECT SUM(Amount) FROM ORDERS WHERE Country = ‘IN’. 
If the executable query is ‘IN’ = 5% of rows (selectivity 5%), the cost of fetching data from a row 
store table is as follows: Case A: Complete table scan: Bytes read ≈ rows × row_size = 100,000,000 
× 72B = 7.2 GB. However, only 11% of that is required by the query, which only requires one 
column (Amount). Thus, nearly 90% of what is read is meaningless. It also means more CPU work 
and slower performance. 
Case B: Applying a B-tree index to the Country. Using the index, find the 5% matching = 
5,000,000 row IDs. The base table’s bytes touched are approximately 360 MB, or 5,000,000 × 
72B. In addition to the CPU overhead for random pointers, index pages are read in tens to hundreds 
of MB. Even though there are fewer total bytes than a full scan, performance can still lag a tight 
sequential column scan due to random access + cache misses. 
Data fetch cost in a column store table: Each column is stored independently in a column-based 
database. Therefore, it only reads the necessary columns (Country and Amount) for the same 
query. Bytes read ≈ rows × row_size = Amount column → 100 million × 8 bytes = 800 MB + 
Country column → 100 million × 1 byte = 100 MB.

To figure out which rows belong to “IN,” it first scans the country (100 MB). After that, it adds 
up only the rows that are marked after scanning the Amount column up to 800 MB. The CPU 
operates very efficiently because this data is sequentially stored and processed in batches. Parts of 
the data may even be ignored if it is compressed or grouped, which would lower the read size to 
less than 900 MB. Therefore, a column store requires only about 900 MB of tightly packed, easily 
readable data rather than 7.2 GB as a row store does. This makes it approximately eight times 
faster and much more CPU-friendly.

4.2. Parallel Processing 
To distribute work among numerous processors, SAP S/4 HANA makes use of distributed nodes 
and multi-core CPUs. A query can be divided into several smaller, concurrently running subtasks 
[6]. For instance, HANA divides the work if you query annual sales totals across regions. “North 
America” is handled by one core, “Europe” by another, etc. The execution time is cut from minutes 
to seconds by instantly combining all of the results.

4.3. Hybrid OLTP + OLAP (Translytical Processing) 
Businesses used to have two distinct databases in older systems: one for OLTP (Online Transaction 
Processing), which managed routine tasks like making sales orders or updating inventory, and 
another for OLAP (Online Analytical Processing), which managed reporting and data analysis [7]. 
Businesses had to transfer transactional data from the OLTP system to the OLAP data warehouse, 
typically overnight, because these systems were independent. Data delays resulted from this, so 
dashboards and reports would constantly display data from the day before rather than the present. 
SAP S/4 HANA changes this completely by combining both OLTP and OLAP capabilities in a

4.4. Push-Down Processing 
Most of the business logic and computations in traditional SAP systems were managed by the 
application server using ABAP code. The primary function of the database was to store and retrieve 
information. This meant that the system had to retrieve a lot of raw data from the database, send it 
over the network to the application server, and then loop through it there to compute results 
whenever you needed to calculate something, like the total sales per product [8]. This data back-

and-forth movement resulted in a high network load, decreased system performance, and resource 
waste. Push-down processing is a concept that SAP S/4 HANA uses to alter this model. The logic 
itself is “pushed down” into the database layer so that HANA performs the computations directly 
inside memory, where the data already exists, instead of extracting all of the data from the database 
for processing. HANA can perform complex aggregations, joins, and filters far faster than an 
external application layer because it is an in-memory, columnar, parallel-processing engine. 
For instance, an older system may loop through millions of records in ABAP if a Fiori dashboard 
needs to display the total revenue for each product. However, with HANA, the aggregation is done 
directly in-memory by the HANA engine, and this logic can be specified in a SQL Script procedure 
or a Core Data Services (CDS) view. The raw data is not returned to the application, and but only 
the final summarized result is returned. 
4.4.1. Performance at the S/4 HANA database layer depends on three critical aspects: Query 
design, index utilization and table partitioning 
a) Query Design 
Push-down processing and set-based logic must be utilized in query design. It will only retrieve 
the necessary data and avoid retrieving a large amount of data. To retrieve the result set in a single 
pass, developers shall use joins, CDS views, or FOR ALL ENTRIES. Instead of using ABAP, the 
database will be used for the calculations and aggregations [8].  
Rather than looping, 
SELECT * FROM zsales INTO TABLE lt_sales.  
LOOP AT lt_sales INTO ls_sales.  
SELECT SINGLE * FROM zcustomer WHERE cust_id = ls_sales-cust_id.  
ENDLOOP.  
 
Query should use a join or CDS view. 
SELECT a.cust_id, b.name, a.amount FROM zsales AS a INNER JOIN zcustomer AS b ON 
a.cust_id = b.cust_id. 
Use CDS views, AMDP, and SQLScript to perform database-layer aggregations, filters, and 
computations. Only necessary columns and filtered rows should be retrieved, and unnecessary 
temporary tables or internal table transfers should be avoided. 
In S/4HANA, designing queries is typically done using CDS (Core Data Services) views. A 
layered view model, such as Interface Views (I_) for raw data access, should serve as the basis for 
CDS. Consumption Views (Z_ or Y_) for analytical exposure (OData/Fiori), and Composite Views 
(C_) for joins and enrichments. Annotate with @Analytics.query: true for analytical queries. Use 
Associations instead of direct joins for flexibility and readability. Apply filters as early as possible 
(prefer WHERE over HAVING). Reduce the number of joins. Don’t join large tables too often. 
Use CDS associations and turn on filter pushdown for hierarchy data. To avoid Cartesian products, 
always verify the cardinality (1:1, 1:N). Make use of CDS’s built-in HANA functions and 
expressions. Use SQL functions (SUM, COUNT, AVG, RANK, CASE, etc.) in place of complex

b) Index Utilization 
Dictionary encoding is already present in every column of a column store, serving as an embedded 
lightweight index. But when filters are complicated or combine several columns, this is insufficient 
on its own. Text search, pattern matching, and join optimization across big tables all depend on 
indexes. HANA comes in different optimized forms, such as inverted indexes, full-text indexes, 
and Multicolumn indexes, each designed for specific data types and query patterns [10].

Inverted Index 
 
Figure 6: Inverted Index [11]  
Figure 6 illustrates how SAP S/4 HANA effectively uses dictionary encoding and an inverted 
index to store column data. Each distinct artist (such as Adele, BTS, or Lady Gaga) is assigned a

the artists’ Value IDs for every row rather than their names, which are stored repeatedly. This 
mapping is inverted by the inverted index, which lists every Value ID along with all the Row IDs 
in which it occurs (Lady Gaga → rows 2, 6).

iii) 
Multicolumn Index 
 
Figure 8: Multi-Column Index 
This Figure 8 illustrates how SAP S/4 HANA assigns a Value ID to each distinct pair of combined 
columns (Region and Product) using a composite dictionary. Each row is mapped to its Value ID 
by the Vector, and this mapping is reversed by the Inverted Index, which enables HANA to quickly 
find rows that match a particular combination. 
Inverted Value Indexes: When searching across several columns at once, SAP S/4 HANA’s 
inverted value index speeds up the database’s ability to locate data. Internally constructs a 
dictionary to hold every possible value combination. A vector that provides numeric IDs for each 
row in place of those values. Those IDs map to the original rows via an inverted index [13]. 
Inverted Has Index: As the vector continues to map each row to its Value ID, it substitutes short 
hash codes for the dictionary’s lengthy combined strings. This uses significantly less memory 
while maintaining the same functionality as a standard inverted index. It stores a hash value, which 
is a brief, fixed-length code that represents the values in each column, rather than the entire 
combined string of all the values in those columns [13]. 
Inverted Individual Index: An inverted individual index uses less memory than an inverted index 
because it does not generate a distinct internal concatenated key column. Rather, it creates small, 
distinct inverted index structures for every column in a multi-column index. Large primary or 
unique indexes with one highly selective column—often used in WHERE clauses—are the ideal 
options for this use. Because less data is written, this index type improves insert, update, and delete 
performance; however, read queries (such as joins or key lookups) may be 10 - 20% slower than 
inverted value indexes [13]. 
Best practices for indexes 
Selecting the appropriate index type is crucial. 
Inverted Value: Use this when you need the fastest read and join performance on primary keys, 
unique constraints, or other hot query paths. Inverted Hash: Avoid using this for non-unique

up DML and reduce memory usage by using lightweight per-column indexes without a 
concatenated key. Reads (PK lookups, filters, and joins) will likely be 10 - 20% slower, which is 
fine for situations where data is accessed infrequently or in bulk [14]. 
To optimize index selectivity and skip-scans, create composite (multicolumn) keys by arranging 
columns so that the most selective equality predicates appear first, followed by other equality 
columns, and then any range or sorting fields. To facilitate effective merge/hash joins and avoid 
redundant conversions, make sure join columns are mirrored in the same order and data types on 
both sides of the relationship. For instance, use (BUKRS, BELNR) consistently in both the header 
and the item tables. A well-designed composite index reduces optimizer confusion and writes 
overhead, and it performs better and requires less maintenance than many single-column secondary 
indexes in the majority of workloads. 
When the target columns have low selectivity, such as Booleans or status flags with few distinct 
values, avoid creating a secondary index because you add write and memory overhead and the 
optimizer gains little. If an existing primary key or unique index path already covers all of the 
predicates, skip the additional indexes because they won’t enhance access plans. Instead of adding 
secondary indexes, which won’t significantly aid scan-heavy queries, concentrate on improving 
CDS logic, partitioning strategy, or preaggregation/materialization if full or analytical scans 
account for the majority of the workload. 
Create an index only when necessary. You can concentrate on the few SQL statements that control 
end-to-end runtime by using the Expensive Statement Trace to find the statements that are either 
the slowest or executed most frequently. Then, use Performance Trace and Plan Viz to drill down 
into those candidates and check for predicate selectivity, join order, join type, and whether 
calculations, projections, and filters are being passed down to HANA in the right way. Next, 
validate your findings across layers: use ST05 to verify database-side index usage and actual bound 
values; use ST12 (and Gateway traces if applicable) to correlate ABAP or OData call stacks with 
the slow SQL; and examine ST03N/STAD to determine workload distribution, peak times, and 
whether the problem is specific to users, transactions, or times of day [15].

c) Table Partitioning 
Data is spread across multiple servers in a multiple-host SAP S/4 HANA system to enhance 
scalability and performance. HANA allows for various data distribution methods. Each index 
server is usually assigned to a separate host [16].  Partitioned tables are divided into multiple 
partitions, each of which may be kept on a separate index server. The load can be balanced by 
allocating different tables to various servers. By enabling the same table to be present on several 
servers, table replication speeds up joins and queries. The various partitioning methods include 
i) Hash Partitioning 
Hash partitioning is used to get around the 2 billion row limit and divide rows evenly among 
partitions for load balancing. Each distinct key value is mapped to one partition based on the hash 
result, ensuring even distribution of rows [16]. The primary purposes of hash partitioning are to: 
properly distribute data among hosts in a multiple-node system. Boosts the execution of parallel 
queries by having each node scan its local partition. Because every partition manages distinct data 
slices, there is less competition for inserts and updates. Maintain manageable partition sizes while 
enabling large-table scalability. 
Query for Hash partitioning, 
CREATE COLUMN TABLE ZSALES_DATA ( 
   SALES_ID     BIGINT, 
   CUSTOMER_ID  INT, 
   REGION       NVARCHAR(20), 
   AMOUNT       DECIMAL(15,2) 
) 
PARTITION BY HASH (CUSTOMER_ID) PARTITIONS 8; 
Here, each CUSTOMER_ID is hashed internally by HANA, which then allocates the row to one 
of 8th partitions. 
ii) Round-Robin Partitioning 
In this case, rows are evenly and sequentially divided among partitions in a round-robin fashion 
[16]. For example, first row in partition 1, second row in partition 2, third row in partition 3, fourth 
row in partition 1, and so forth. In situations where there is no natural partitioning key (no suitable 
column for hash or range), round-robin partitioning works best. When it comes to bulk loads or 
analytics, you want parallelism and balanced data. There is no selective filtering; query patterns 
search through all tables. Because the rows are spread out across all partitions, it is inefficient for 
key-filtering queries.

 Best practices in partitioning 
Range partitioning is the default choice for time-series or housekeeping data, where most queries 
filter by a chronological or sequential column such as CALMONTH, DOC_DATE, or LOAD_TS. 
By using this method, the database can perform partitioning, which significantly improves 
performance by examining only the relevant date ranges when executing queries. Because entire 
partitions can be merged or deleted without affecting active ones, this also makes lifecycle 
operations, such as archiving or dropping old data, easier. However, a composite range-hash 
strategy is advised if recent time ranges accumulate disproportionate data (hot partitions). This 
involves dividing by time range first, followed by hash sub-partitioning for even load distribution. 
Hash partitioning is used for key-based access patterns, such as when queries frequently filter on 
high-cardinality columns like CUSTOMER_ID or DOC_ID. It guarantees that data is distributed 
evenly across nodes or partitions. This method helps scale workloads horizontally by supporting 
parallel processing during large joins and scans.

5. CONCLUSION 
The goal of this study was to clarify how the in-memory database layer of SAP S/4HANA provides 
high performance and to convert those architectural concepts into useful optimization techniques 
for actual enterprise systems. The study demonstrates that many SAP performance bottlenecks can 
be reduced when the database layer is intentionally built rather than viewed as a passive storage 
component by looking at columnar storage, dictionary and vector compression, parallel 
processing, hybrid OLTP/OLAP behavior, push-down processing, indexing, and table partitioning 
in a single unified framework. These design decisions are not just conceptual, as the comparative 
metrics between ECC and HANA environments show they lead to significant decreases in data 
scanned, query runtime, network transfer, and application-server load.  
The paper connects theoretical concepts like compressed dictionaries, vectorized scans, and 
translytical processing to their practical implementation in S/4HANA, building on fundamental 
research in in-memory and column-store databases. Simultaneously, real-world proof of how 
query design, index selection, and partition strategy impact execution plans, CPU utilization, and 
end-to-end response times is provided by practical experiments using SQL Script, CDS views, and 
ABAP comparisons—measured via ST05, ST12, SAT, DBACOCKPIT, and Plan Viz. A gap in

previous work, which frequently describes HANA capabilities but does not quantify their runtime 
impact in realistic S/4HANA workloads, is filled by this dual theoretical - practical approach. 
The results advise practitioners to treat indexing and partitioning as primary tuning levers in line 
with workload patterns, prioritize set-based database push-down via CDS and SQL Script rather 
than ABAP loops, and integrate performance engineering into implementation lifecycles by 
methodically using trace and analysis tools. Strategically, the findings indicate that while clean-
core and modular CDS practices keep systems upgrade-safe and cloud-ready, utilizing hybrid 
OLTP/OLAP capabilities enables organizations to simplify landscapes, eliminate ETL latency, 
and enable real-time Fiori and analytics directly on operational data. The evidence presented here 
suggests that enterprises can consistently achieve high-performance, real-time processing at scale 
when S/4HANA’s in-memory architecture is paired with disciplined query, index, and partition 
design. Future research can expand this measurement framework to specific industry scenarios, 
multi-tenant cloud setups, and AI-driven workloads.

Abstract: Aim: The study aims to investigate how SAP S/4HANA’s in-memory database architecture achieves exceptionally high processing speeds by examining the HANA database layer, where most SAP system performance challenges originate. It further seeks to analyze how columnar storage, compression techniques, set-based programming, indexing, and data-partitioning strategies contribute to overall system efficiency, scalability, and real-time analytics. Methods: The research is grounded in SAP HANA architecture documentation, S/4HANA developer manuals, and established performance-engineering literature. A practical assessment was conducted using representative SQL queries, CDS Views, and SQL Scripts executed directly on SAP HANA. Performance-analysis tools included ST05, ST12, SAT, DBACOCKPIT, and PlanViz to evaluate memory usage, indexing behavior, execution paths, and runtime performance. Results: The study reveals that SAP S/4HANA’s columnar storage model significantly enhances selective data retrieval, while dictionary and vector-based compression reduce memory footprint and accelerate data access. Storing operational data entirely in main memory enables simultaneous execution of transactional and analytical workloads. Set-based processing through CDS Views and SQL Script is shown to outperform traditional ABAP loop-based logic, reinforcing the effectiveness of shifting computations to the database layer. Additionally, partitioning strategies such as round-robin, hash, and range partitioning enable parallel execution and even distribution of large datasets across processing threads, improving scalability and sustaining performance under heavy workloads. Conclusion: The study concludes that SAP S/4HANA’s in-memory design combined with columnar processing, advanced compression, database-driven logic, and optimized indexing and partitioning forms the foundation of its real-time processing capability. Recommendation: To fully leverage S/4HANA’s performance potential, developers and solution architects should adopt set-based programming practices, apply appropriate indexing and partitioning strategies, and rely on database-side execution wherever possible.
